meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Squeaky Wheel Gets the Grease'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Josh Billings by Bartlett’s in 1937, with no source. The verse is Cal Stewart’s, published 1903 and confirmed in the scan.

answer.label: Not Josh Billings — actually Cal Stewart
answer.authorDates: 1856–1919 · American vaudeville comedian and recording artist
answer.sourceLine: The proverb comes from a verse by the vaudeville comedian Cal Stewart, printed as the epigraph to Uncle Josh Weathersby’s ‘Punkin Centre’ Stories in 1903 and signed with the name of his fictional storyteller, Josh Weathersby. We read it in the scanned 1905 edition, whose copyright page confirms the 1903 date. The long-standing credit to the humorist Josh Billings appears to be a confusion of two Joshes: Quote Investigator suggests “some previous researcher confused the fictional character Josh Weathersby with the penname Josh Billings”. Note the familiar six-word proverb is a later condensation — Stewart’s own line is “the wheel what squeaks the loudest is the one what gets the grease”.

source.excerpt:
“I don’t believe in kickin’,
It aint apt to bring one peace;
But the wheel what squeaks the loudest
Is the one what gets the grease.”
— Josh Weathersby.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ is the anchor, and its verdict is unambiguous: “based on current evidence this adage should be credited to Cal Stewart and not to Josh Billings.” QI gives the earliest appearance as the 1903 Stewart collection, page 6.

We confirmed that against the book itself rather than taking it on trust. The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1905 Thompson & Thomas edition ↗ carries the four-line verse on its epigraph leaf, signed “— Josh Weathersby”, and its copyright page reads “Copyright, 1903 By W. L. Eckhardt and Calvin E. Stewart” — independently fixing the 1903 first-publication date that the public-domain status rests on.

On the Billings credit, QI cites The Yale Book of Quotations noting that the existence of “The Kicker”, the poem Billings supposedly wrote it in, “has never been verified”, and says the ascription entered the eleventh edition of Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations in 1937 with no supporting citation. Josh Billings was the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw, 1818–1885 ↗.

QI also documents genuine precursors with different meanings — Franklin’s “The worst wheel of the cart makes the most noise” in Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1737, and a 1796 House of Commons remark by Sheridan about greasing “that squeaking wheel in the city” — so the image is older than Stewart even though this phrasing is his.

One negative result worth recording: Project Gutenberg’s e-text of the Punkin Centre stories ↗ does not contain the verse — we searched its full text and found no instance of “squeak” or “kickin”. Its transcription omits the epigraph leaf, so it cannot be used to confirm this quotation. The 1905 scan can.

author.name: Cal Stewart
author.heading: About Cal Stewart
author.metaLine: 1856–1919 · American vaudeville comedian and pioneering recording artist
author.bio: Cal Stewart (1856–1919) was an American comedian and humorist who pioneered both vaudeville monologue and early sound recording — his own book billed him as “The Talking Machine Story Teller”. He is best remembered for Uncle Josh Weathersby, a garrulous old resident of the invented New England village of Punkin Centre, whose stories Stewart sold in print and on cylinder records to a national audience. He signed the verse behind this proverb with his character’s name rather than his own, which is most likely why the credit went astray.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: One wrong name has dominated this proverb for nearly ninety years, and it seems to be a mix-up between two humorists both called Josh.

items.why: The ascription entered Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations in its 1937 eleventh edition without a citation, and reference works have copied it since. QI reports ↗ that The Yale Book of Quotations finds the poem it supposedly comes from, “The Kicker”, has never been verified to exist. QI’s explanation is a confusion between Stewart’s character Josh Weathersby and the pen name Josh Billings.
Lardner printed a version of the verse in the Chicago Tribune in July 1913, but he marked it “ANON.” himself — as QI records ↗ — so he made no claim on it.

Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1737 has “The worst wheel of the cart makes the most noise”, which QI calls a precursor with a distinct meaning ↗ — about the weakest part complaining most, not about complaint being rewarded.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict ↗: credit Cal Stewart, 1903 — not Josh Billings. The modern six-word form is a condensation of his four-line verse.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cal Stewart was one of the first recording stars: his “Uncle Josh” monologues sold on cylinders and discs to people who had never seen a vaudeville stage, and the title page of his own book bills him as “The Talking Machine Story Teller”. Putting the verse in a rustic character’s mouth is what made it portable — folk wisdom needs a folk source.

The irony is that the device worked too well. Because Stewart signed the epigraph “Josh Weathersby” rather than with his own name, the proverb drifted to a different Josh entirely, and a reference book made the error permanent in 1937. The character outlived its author’s claim to his own line.
context.pull: Folk wisdom needs a folk source — and Stewart’s worked so well it cost him the credit.

QI gives the earliest appearance as Uncle Josh Weathersby's 'Punkin Centre' stories by Cal Stewart, 1903, page 6, Regan Printing House, Chicago, with the four-line verse signed 'Josh Weathersby'.

QI reports that the Yale Book of Quotations notes the existence of 'The Kicker', the poem Billings supposedly wrote, has never been verified, and that the Billings ascription entered Bartlett's eleventh edition in 1937 with no citation.

QI documents Franklin's 1737 Poor Richard precursor 'The worst wheel of the cart makes the most noise' and Sheridan's 1796 House of Commons remark about greasing 'that squeaking wheel in the city', both with distinct meanings, and Ring Lardner's July 1913 Chicago Tribune printing labelled 'ANON.'

The scanned 1905 Thompson & Thomas edition carries the verse on its epigraph leaf signed '— Josh Weathersby', bills Cal Stewart as 'The Talking Machine Story Teller', and its copyright page reads 'Copyright, 1903 By W. L. Eckhardt and Calvin E. Stewart'. Read directly by quotle.info.
Cal Stewart was an American comedian and humorist who lived 1856 to 1919 and created the Uncle Josh Weathersby character of Punkin Center.
Josh Billings was the pen name of Henry Wheeler Shaw, an American humorist who lived 1818 to 1885.
